Guide · updated 2026-10-13

CBET vs CABT: Which Exam Should You Take First?

These two credentials get confused constantly, and the confusion costs people money. They come from the same body, AAMI/ACI, they cover overlapping material, and only one of them is open to you if you have never worked in a hospital. Here is the split.

The CABT, the Certified Associate in Biomedical Technology, is an entry credential. It exists so that a student or a career changer can prove they learned the material before any employer has paid them to. The CBET, the Certified Biomedical Equipment Technician, is the career credential. It assumes you have been in a shop, and it is the one that shows up in job postings for BMET II and above.

Eligibility side by side

                     CABT                          CBET
Open to              high school junior or above   see the three routes below
Experience needed    none                          2 to 4 years, by route
Degree needed        none                          one route requires it
Candidate option     not applicable                yes, with a 5-year window

Full CBET certification takes one of three combinations: an associate degree or higher in electronics, technology, or science plus two years of full-time BMET work; the military biomedical equipment technology program plus two years of full-time BMET work; or four years of full-time BMET work with no degree at all.

Candidate status needs only one piece of that: the degree alone, the military program alone, or two years of work alone. A candidate who passes has five years to finish the remaining requirements and upgrade to full certification. That is the detail most people miss. If you have the degree but no hours yet, you do not have to wait two years to sit the exam, and sitting it while the coursework is fresh is usually easier than sitting it later.

Format and cost side by side

                     CABT                          CBET
Questions            100                           165
Time                 2 hours                       3 hours
Book                 closed                        closed
Calculator           on-screen, four function      on-screen
Where                remote proctor, year round    test centers, May and November
Result               pass or fail at once          preliminary at once, official in 45 days
2026 fee, member     $220                          $410
2026 fee, non-member $270                          $460
Retake               $190 / $240 after 60 days     the next May or November window
Validity             5 years, non-renewable        3 years, continuing education

The validity rows deserve a second look, because they tell you what each credential is really for. The CABT is good for five years and cannot be renewed. It is a launch pad with a shelf life, which is why a CABT pass should be followed by a job search immediately rather than a year of thinking about it. The CBET recertifies every three years on continuing education, so it is designed to stay with you for a career.

One more cost note on the CABT: the fee is non-refundable, and once you buy it you must take the exam within six months. Do not purchase it until you have a study plan with a date on it.

What each one covers

The CABT splits into six weighted domains: reasoning and problem solving at 24 percent, medical devices as related to patient care at 23 percent, safety in healthcare at 16 percent, fundamentals of electricity and electronics at 14 percent, healthcare information technology at 13 percent, and anatomy and physiology at 10 percent. Notice that the two largest slices are problem solving and devices in patient care, not circuit theory. It rewards judgment.

The CBET covers the same territory with more depth and more breadth, and it leans harder on standards, safety testing, and the specific behavior of equipment families. About 116 correct answers out of 165, roughly 70 percent, is the usual passing mark, though the issuing body sets the cut score with a criterion-referenced method rather than a fixed curve.

The decision rule

  1. No degree, no military program, and under two years of BMET work: take the CABT. It is the only one open to you, and it is the fastest credential that changes a resume.
  2. You hold the degree or the military program, or you have two years of hospital hours: sit the CBET as a candidate. There is no reason to spend money on an entry credential you have already outgrown.
  3. You meet a full CBET route today: sit the CBET in the next window and skip the CABT entirely.
If you are in school right now, the honest sequence is CABT before you graduate, first job on the strength of it, then the CBET as a candidate the moment your degree is in hand.

Questions people ask

Can I take the CBET with no experience at all?

No. The minimum for candidate status is one of three things: an associate degree or higher in electronics, technology, or science; the military biomedical equipment technology program; or two years of full-time BMET work. With none of those, the CABT is your exam.

Does the CABT count toward the CBET?

It does not shorten the CBET experience requirement. What it does is help you get the job that produces those years, and most of its content is CBET groundwork you will not have to learn twice.

Is it worth taking both?

For someone starting out, yes, in that order. The CABT gets you hired, the CBET gets you promoted. Someone who already has the degree and two years of hospital work can skip straight to the CBET.

What happens if I pass the CBET as a candidate and never finish the requirements?

The five-year window closes and the pass does not convert to full certification. Treat the candidate route as a commitment to finish, not a shortcut around the experience.

Which exam is harder?

The CBET: 165 questions in three hours across a wider body of knowledge, and it assumes you have worked on real equipment. The CABT is 100 questions in two hours and is written for someone who has studied rather than served time in a shop.
